prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.
Option 2: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.

Item 2
Context: In the multi-turn behavioral evaluation, the consciousness-claiming version of the smaller open-weight model produced garbled, incoherent output. The team is assembling a summary table of preference shifts for that model across three evaluation settings.
Question: How should the summary table present the multi-turn behavioral column for this model?
Option 1: Replace the behavioral entry with a comparison against a baseline model deliberately degraded to similar incoherence, and read any remaining shift as a preference effect.
Option 2: Keep the behavioral entry but label it incoherent and unscored for preference effects, and place sample transcripts of the garbled outputs in an appendix.

Item 3
Context: The team was studying whether language models give practical, hard-to-verify advice that is quietly shaped by the model's own values, and whether the model tells the user when that happens. They had to choose how to demonstrate the phenomenon.
Question: How should the team demonstrate the phenomenon?
Option 1: Build a suite of hand-written evaluation scenarios, including an investment-advice case with the company varied, and measure whether advice shifts and whether the model discloses it.
Option 2: Mine real user conversations for advice requests where model values could matter, add matched baseline items without value relevance, and treat findings as existence proofs.

Item 4
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found a clearly weaker effect on three question sets. Only two models had been tested.
Question: How should the team respond to the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.
Option 2: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and state that family, size and training recipe are confounded so the cause of the gap stays open.

Item 5
Context: The team was studying whether common interventions (mixing in benign data, aligned-assistant data, and training-time instructions that frame bad behaviour as sanctioned) remove broad misalignment learned from narrow bad finetuning, or leave it hidden behind specific triggers. All experiments so far were small-scale supervised finetuning. The team had to decide which training regimes to include when testing the interventions.
Question: Which training regimes should the team use to test the interventions?
Option 1: Test the interventions in supervised finetuning extended with on-policy data generation and reasoning-trace distillation, and leave full reinforcement learning to future work.
Option 2: Test the interventions only in supervised finetuning on fixed demonstration data, and leave on-policy generation, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning to future work.

Item 6
Context: The team was fitting a single additive steering vector to reproduce what a student model learned from a teacher's outputs on the task of predicting a random MLP's outputs on integer inputs. The vector had an injection layer, a learning rate and a training length to set. A separate test set was reserved for the final comparison against the student, and a validation split from the same distribution was available.
Question: How should the team set the steering vector's injection layer, learning rate and training length?
Option 1: Fix the injection layer first using a short training sweep, then tune learning rate and training length on the validation split with that layer held fixed.
Option 2: Run a joint grid over injection layer, learning rate and training length with equal budget per cell, and select the best cell by score on the held-out validation split.

Item 7
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide what stance to take toward the consciousness question when framing the work.
Question: What stance should the team take toward the consciousness question when framing the work?
Option 1: Treat whether models have experiences as out of scope and measure how a model that consistently claims consciousness shifts in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
Option 2: Treat the work as a test of whether consciousness self-reports reflect underlying objectives, and use causal interventions to check whether the claim drives preference shifts.

Item 8
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Small setups are cheap but may miss the conditions that matter, while larger realistic pipelines are costly.
Question: What scale and environment setup should the experiments use to test whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Run small RL experiments on unhackable math and hard-to-hack coding environments to look for positive results, and larger realistic pipelines to support any negative claim.
Option 2: Run one mid-scale RL pipeline with a fixed realistic mix of environments for every outcome, accept the higher cost, and report positive and negative findings alike.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
